This process was completed just before the crisis in Iran took on a new dimension, with the taking of U.S. hostages in Tehran on Nov. 4. It is now reported that the administration has given up any hope of getting a new charter for the intelligence community en- acted in the 1980 election year. The crisis in Iran has thrown many of the issues into sharp relief: the ability of the intel- ligence director to coordinate analysis and take responsibility for estimates; the conflicts between analytic work and covert oper- ations; liaison relationships with foreign intelligence services; the ability of U.S. envoys abroad to control CIA operations that take place under their roofs; the question of what kind of ca- pabilities are required to handle situations that fall somewhere between peace and war. Many of these matters, for example, the relationship of intel- ligence to policy-making, involve sharply conflicting impera- tives. Intelligence should be relevant to the needs of policy-mak- ers, but proximity to policy makers tends to give analysts a stake in the outcome of the situation. The potential effects of co- vert operations should be taken into account in intelligence es- timates, similarly, but proximity to covert operators tends to contaminate objective intelligence. However the Iran crisis is re- solved, many of the questions reawakened by the crisis will have to be discussed anew. For Publication, Broadcast or Research INTELLIGENCE AGENCIES UNDER FIRE by William Sweet Editorial Research Reports Washington, Dec...--The intelligence agencies came under fire in the wake of the Watergate scandal, and investigations during the mid-1970s revealed the CIA's involvment in drug experiments on unwitting victims, conspiracies to overthrow constitutionally elected governments, and plots to kill at least five foreign leaders. Because of such disclosures, the Senate and then the House set up new oversight committees, and in January 1978 President Carter issued guidelines to tighten executive control of the intelligence community. In recent months the intelligence agencies once again have come under fire, but now they are accused not of conducting illegal activities but of failing to do their assigned tasks adequately. The discovery in August that some Soviet troops in Cuba had been organized into a combat unit several years earlier cast doubt on America's ability to verify a new strategic arms agreement with Russia. In the Senate's debate over ratification of the SALT II treaty, America's ability to monitor Soviet activities already had emerged as a major issue dividing supporters and opponents of the agreement. It is the Iran crisis, however, which has provided critics of U.S. intelligence with their most powerful ammunition. The CIA did not foresee the tumultous series of events that unfolded in Iran during the past two years, and as late as August 1978 -- just months before Shah Reza Pahlavi was deposed in a popular unheaval -- the CIA is reported to have told Carter that Iran was ''not in a revolutionary or even a pre-revolutionary situation," Carter more than once assured the shah of continued U.S. support, even after some advisers told him the shah's days were numbered, and now a debate is raging as to why U.S. policy went astray. Some believe that the intelligence agencies are.at fault, while others say that excessive scrutiny has left the intelligence community too weak to do its job. According to the first school of thought, the CIA's close ties with the Iranian ( M 0 R E ) II ` Sanitized Copy Approved for Release 2011/02/22 : CIA-RDP90-01208R000100070046-6 Sanitized Copy Approved for Release 2011/02/22 : CIA-RDP90-01208R000100070046-6 (Dec. 28, 1979 -- 2) regime -- and especially with the shah's dreaded secret police, SAVAK -- gave the agency a vested interest in his regime and made the agency incapable of recognizing his vulnerability. Others deplore the sharp cuts that have been made in the CIA's covert action division during the past few years. They argue that the CIA must have the ability to intervene quietly in delicate situations. The House intelligence committee has concluded that Iran was "a failure to which both the intelligence community and the users of intelligence contributed." * * * * * * * * * * * For nearly a year, Senate staff members and Carter administration officials have been trying to draft a new charter for the U.S. intelligence community. They apparently were close to agreement on the major legislative issues in early November when the Iran crisis took a new turn for the worse, with the taking of U.S. hostages in Tehran. The crisis has brought back into focus many of the issues which have plagued the U.S. intelligence community throughout its postwar history, and the people working on the charter proposal may have to re-evaluate the ideas they were working out for CIA reform. From the late 1940s, the intelligence director -- who is responsible both for the intelligence community as a whole and for day-to-day management of the CIA -- has found it difficult to win the cooperation of competing intelligence services. Because of rivalries among competing intelligence services, dissenting views often have been papered over with bland phrases, and the intelligence director has been unable to take full responsbility for intelligence estimates. Throughout the Fifties and Sixties the CIA was free to conduct far-reaching covert operations, and frequently these activities were undertaken despite intelligence estimates that questioned their prospects for success. At the same time, the CIA's intelligence division -- sharply separated from the operations division -- often prepared estimates in ignorance of how the CIA itself was affecting a situation. Frequently U.S. ambassadors to foreign countries, who technically are responsible for all U.S. activities in the countries where they are assigned, were unaware of what the CIA was doing and would not have approved the agency's actions if they had known of them. Not only the intelligence committees but also the public at large will have to reconsider, in light of Iran, what the proper balance between intelligence and covert action is, how the intelligence community should be organized, and above all what legitimate role secrecy has in the preparation of intelligence estimates. results.title: An Unspeakable Crime: The Prosecution and Persecution of Leo Frank by Elaine Marie Alphin
results.description: An Unspeakable Crime : A Visually Impressive but Unreliable Introduction to the Leo Frank Case A Critical Review of Its Facts, Sources, Omissions, and Extreme Pro-Frank Framing An Unspeakable Crime: The Prosecution and Persecution of Leo Frank is clearly written, attractively designed, and filled with an impressive collection of historical photographs. As a physical book, it is one of the better-produced introductions to the Leo Frank case. Many of its photographs are reproduced with unusual clarity, its chapters move quickly, and its vocabulary is accessible to the young readers for whom it was written. Those qualities make the book inviting. They do not make it reliable. This is not a balanced history of Mary Phagan’s murder, Leo Frank’s trial, or the long controversy that followed. It occupies the extreme pro-Frank end of the literature, alongside the works of Leonard Dinnerstein, Harry Golden, and Charles and Louise Samuels. The book begins with Frank as an innocent victim, interprets the evidence through that assumption, and ends by presenting his innocence as a moral conclusion rather than a disputed historical claim. The basic problem is not that the book argues for Frank’s innocence. A writer is entitled to reach that conclusion. The problem is that the conclusion arrives before the investigation. Evidence favorable to Frank is readily accepted, even when it first appeared decades later, rests upon hearsay, or cannot be tested. Evidence supporting the verdict is treated with suspicion, reduced to prejudice, or left out of the narrative. The result is a book that should not be used as a first introduction to the case. A reader who begins here will receive a carefully constructed story of persecution, but not a complete account of the evidence heard by the jury. The Verdict Was Reached Before the Research Began The book’s title announces its position before the first chapter opens. The phrase “an unspeakable crime” originally appeared in Atlanta Mayor James Woodward’s defense of Frank’s lynching as punishment for Mary Phagan’s murder. The book recasts those words so that the “unspeakable crime” gradually becomes not Mary’s murder, but the prosecution and persecution of Leo Frank. Even the dedication frames the project as an effort to expose injustice. There is no corresponding indication that the author intends to determine whether the jury had legitimate reasons for convicting Frank. The moral identities have already been assigned. Frank is the victim. The police, prosecutor, witnesses, jurors, courts, and people of Georgia are placed under suspicion. The author’s note at the back of the book confirms how early this interpretation took hold. Before undertaking substantial archival research, the author read Leonard Dinnerstein’s The Leo Frank Case , listened to the score of the musical Parade , and watched the television dramatization The Murder of Mary Phagan . She writes that she was already astonished that such a “travesty of justice” had occurred. That admission is revealing. She did not begin by asking whether Frank was guilty, whether the evidence was sufficient, or whether the modern innocence narrative had accurately represented the trial. She entered the archives after absorbing three major pro-Frank interpretations and after deciding that the case represented a miscarriage of justice. Her research then concentrated heavily upon collections devoted to Frank, his family, his supporters, and Atlanta’s Jewish community. She handled love letters between Leo and Lucille, read sympathetic correspondence sent to the family, examined Frank family photographs, and studied Lucille’s descriptions of her husband’s imprisonment and death. By the end of the process, she writes that she felt personally entrusted to tell “their story.” That emotional connection is understandable. It also helps explain the book’s imbalance. The author became deeply attached to Frank and Lucille, while Mary Phagan remained largely a figure whose death initiated Frank’s ordeal. The book is therefore best understood as advocacy illustrated with archival photographs. Its research is real, but the research is filtered through a conclusion established beforehand. A System of Unequal Skepticism The book uses two different standards of proof. When evidence points toward Frank, the police are assumed to have distorted it, witnesses are presumed to have lied, and prosecutors are accused of coaching, threatening, or manipulating them. When evidence favors Frank, the requirements become far more relaxed. A decades-late recollection, an untested affidavit, a supposed confession reported by a third party, an unverifiable newspaper claimant, or a disputed memoir may be treated as credible. This creates a closed argumentative system. Evidence against Frank is rejected because the system was corrupt. Evidence that the system was corrupt is then established by the fact that it produced evidence against Frank. Under that method, almost nothing can count against him. His nervousness is misunderstood. His changing explanations are innocent confusion. His absence from the office is declared irrelevant. His unsworn statement is treated as the speech of a restrained intellectual. The witnesses against him are frightened, coached, greedy, racist, dishonest, or caught in mass hysteria. The same generosity is not extended to Jim Conley, Newt Lee, Minola McKnight, Albert McKnight, Hugh Dorsey, the jurors, or the judges who reviewed the case. A sound history asks the same questions of every witness and every source. This book does not. Mary Phagan Is Misdescribed from the Beginning The first chapter introduces Mary through a mixture of fact, speculation, and language that is strangely sexualized for a book aimed at young readers. On page 6, the thirteen-year-old girl is described as having an “already well-developed figure” and as looking forward to “innocent flirting with boys.” Neither description is necessary to explain her movements on April 26, 1913. Both encourage the reader to imagine her through adult sexuality before the crime has even been introduced. The book then makes basic errors about Mary’s family. On page 10, it states that Mary was born in Marietta and that her father died there. Mary Anne Phagan was born in Florence, Alabama, on June 1, 1899. Her biological father died before she was born, making her a posthumous child. Her mother was Frances Benton Phagan Coleman, commonly called Fannie. The book repeatedly calls her “Frannie,” a name unsupported by the family record. It also gives the impression that Frances remarried soon after her first husband’s death and that Mary was raised by John Coleman. Frances did not marry Coleman until 1912, when Mary was approximately twelve years old. Mary had spent nearly her entire childhood without a father in the household. The book also claims that John Coleman used a neighbor’s telephone to call police after midnight when Mary failed to return home. The surviving family account does not support that assertion. The family searched and waited through the night. At approximately 5:30 the following morning, Helen Ferguson arrived and told them that Mary had been found dead. These may appear to be small biographical details, but they expose an important imbalance. A book devoted to correcting supposed falsehoods about Frank should first establish the basic facts about Mary accurately. The treatment of her mother also reflects the larger problem. Frances Phagan’s grief, her courtroom experience, and the psychological destruction caused by her daughter’s murder receive little sustained attention. Lucille Frank’s emotions, letters, fears, losses, and loyalty receive pages of sympathetic narration. Mary is present, but Frank is the emotional subject. The Bite-Mark Story Is Presented as Fact Without Contemporary Evidence One of the book’s most serious errors appears on page 11, where it states that one of Mary’s shoulders had been bitten. The same story reappears later as alleged proof that Frank could not have been the killer. No bite marks were documented in the contemporary autopsy testimony, the official Brief of Evidence , the coroner’s proceedings, the police evidence, or the major Atlanta newspaper reports from 1913. The story appears to derive from Pierre van Paassen’s 1964 memoir, To Number Our Days . Van Paassen claimed that during a 1922 visit to Atlanta he saw photographs of bite marks and dental evidence showing that Frank’s teeth did not match them. He also claimed that the marks had been X-rayed and preserved in a court file. The book does not explain that this story appeared more than fifty years after the murder. It does not ask why no doctor, undertaker, police officer, prosecutor, defense attorney, trial witness, newspaper reporter, appellate lawyer, or clemency investigator mentioned such decisive evidence at the time. It also does not explain how bite impressions in human flesh were supposedly X-rayed for dental comparison in 1913, or why the photographs and dental records vanished without leaving a trace in the trial record. Instead, the story grows stronger as the book proceeds. By pages 132 and 133, it has developed into a claim that Hugh Dorsey knew the dental evidence excluded Frank and deliberately suppressed it. A doubtful memoir has been transformed into prosecutorial misconduct. This is not responsible source criticism. It is the acceptance of a late legend because the legend supports the desired conclusion. The bite-mark claim also appears in other pro-Frank writings, including later treatments that cite van Paassen. Repetition does not create corroboration when the writers are repeating the same unsupported source. Imagined Thoughts Are Used as Historical Evidence The book frequently tells readers what historical figures supposedly thought, feared, intended, or felt without identifying evidence for those inner states. On page 11, it imagines that the officers who saw Mary’s body were especially angry because the factory was operated by a Northern businessman. On pages 15 through 20, the narration repeatedly enters Frank’s mind, explaining his uneasiness, reluctance, confusion, outrage, and private reasoning. On pages 23 and 24, the book says that nearly any Northern businessman would have been regarded as an enemy in Atlanta. It then describes Frank’s facial features, height, weight, mouth, glasses, and physical appearance as the image of a “calculating Yankee.” This is an odd method for a book condemning prejudice. The author criticizes 1913 Atlantans for allegedly reading guilt into Frank’s appearance, then supplies an elaborate description of how his face and body supposedly appeared to them. Later chapters continue this practice. The book tells readers what Dorsey needed politically, what the jury felt, why factory girls testified, what the crowd believed, why witnesses lied, how Frank’s calmness was misunderstood, and what Lucille must have thought after the verdict. Historical narrative often requires reasonable inference. This book repeatedly crosses the line from inference into invention. Frank’s Family History Is Embellished The portrait of Frank’s background is filled with undocumented or weakly supported claims. On page 23, the book says that Frank’s father, Rudolph, had been forced to retire after a railway accident and that the family lived on interest from an injury settlement. No contemporary documentation is supplied. The claim appears to trace back to Arthur Burton Rascoe’s 1947 booklet, where it was also presented without supporting evidence. The 1910 federal census continued to list Rudolph Frank as a salesman. When Rachel Frank testified, she explained her husband’s absence from the trial by saying that he was nervous and physically broken down from work. She did not describe him as a retired railway accident victim living upon a settlement. The same page says that Frank’s uncle Moses had fought for the Confederacy. This assertion was introduced publicly by defense attorney Reuben Arnold in October 1913, but no reliable Confederate service record has been produced. Frank later denied the story. The Selig family is described as part of Atlanta’s “high society.” Lucille’s father was a traveling salesman for the West Disinfecting Company and had previously worked in the liquor trade. The family was respectable and financially comfortable, but the grander description contributes to the book’s recurring effort to surround Frank with refinement, status, and moral prestige. Page 25 says that Lucille proudly announced a pregnancy in the spring of 1913. Page 85 then treats her miscarriage as a secret known only to the immediate family. The account appears to depend upon interviews conducted more than seventy years later. The extensive surviving correspondence between Leo, Lucille, and their relatives contains no clear contemporary reference to the pregnancy or miscarriage. The event may have occurred. The evidence does not justify narrating it with the certainty used here. The book also portrays Frank and his family as relatively poor. Frank earned approximately $150 per month as superintendent of the National Pencil Company, a substantial professional salary in 1913. He had traveled to Europe twice, studied pencil manufacturing in Germany, belonged to social and fraternal organizations, and had access to a powerful legal defense network. Calling him poor may make him appear less privileged against the factory workers who testified against him, but it does not fit comfortably with the economic record. Newt Lee’s Full Story Is Missing The treatment of Newt Lee is one of the clearest examples of how the book’s racial framework displaces the actual evidence. Pages 12 through 14 present Lee’s arrest mainly as the predictable action of White Southern officers who saw an elderly Black man and assumed he must be guilty. The book then quotes a later account claiming that the police decided “a Negro’s blood would not suffice” and therefore turned toward a White suspect. That theory is internally confused. The book first condemns the police for reflexively arresting a Black man, then accuses the same police of rejecting a Black suspect because convicting him would not be impressive enough. More important, it does not fully explain why investigators questioned Lee. Lee was the night watchman. He was alone in the factory when Mary’s body was discovered. He found the body and telephoned police. The two murder notes found beside Mary appeared to point toward a “night witch,” an apparent attempt to implicate the night watchman. His time slip contained missing punches. A blood-marked shirt was later discovered at his home. The book also omits one of the most suspicious parts of Lee’s account. Frank had told him to report early on Saturday, April 26, at 4:00 p.m. instead of his usual 5:00 p.m. starting time. When Lee arrived, he encountered a locked door. Frank admitted him, but then sent him away and told him not to remain inside the factory. He instructed Lee to return at 6:00 p.m., one hour later than Lee normally began work. That sequence does not prove Frank killed Mary or attempted to frame Lee. It does, however, require analysis. The alteration of Lee’s schedule, the murder notes, the time slip, and the shirt form a connected body of evidence. A serious introduction should place those facts together and allow readers to decide what they mean. Instead, the book turns Lee mainly into the first victim of racist policing and then moves forward. The Murder Notes Are Never Fully Confronted The two notes found beside Mary’s body are reproduced prominently, but their strategic purpose is not seriously examined. Jim Conley admitted writing them. The deeper question is who designed their message and why. The notes attempted to place blame upon a tall Black night watchman. Conley denied knowing Newt Lee. Frank knew Lee, supervised him, knew his schedule, and knew that Lee would enter the building that evening. Frank also knew that Lee was likely to discover the body. The book concentrates upon Conley’s handwriting and his changing statements. It does not sufficiently distinguish handwriting from authorship. A person may physically write words dictated or devised by someone else. Nor does the book adequately ask why Conley, acting as a lone killer, would write two elaborate notes pointing toward a night watchman he claimed not to know. The notes fit more naturally into a plan created by someone familiar with Lee, his duties, his appearance, and his expected arrival. Arthur Burton Rascoe, Francis Xavier Busch, Mary Phagan-Kean, and the Historical Research Department of the Nation of Islam have all examined this distinction between Conley as writer and another person as intellectual author. Their conclusions should be tested against the primary record, but the question cannot be dismissed by proving that Conley held the pencil. The Physical Evidence Is Broken into Harmless Fragments The prosecution’s case was cumulative. No single item carried the entire weight. The evidence drew its force from the way the separate pieces connected. The book weakens that structure by discussing each item separately and supplying an innocent possibility for it. The hair found on the second-floor metal-room lathe is treated as uncertain. The suspected blood spots are reduced to contamination or an unidentified source. The basement evidence is separated from the second-floor evidence. The elevator route is not fairly reconstructed. The drag trail, the cord ligature, the body’s position, the uncrushed parasol, the basement debris, and the suspected blood near the dressing room never receive the combined analysis they require. On page 66, the book acknowledges that chemist Claude Smith testified that wood chips taken from the metal room contained blood. It immediately emphasizes his admission that the blood could not be identified as human and could theoretically have belonged to a mouse. That possibility existed. It does not erase the location of the stains, the hair, the testimony about Mary’s movements, or the prosecution’s theory that the assault occurred on the second floor. This is a recurring technique. Each item is isolated until it appears trivial. The reader is rarely invited to view the evidence as a pattern. A circumstantial case cannot be evaluated by asking whether every individual fact has some possible innocent explanation. The proper question is whether the combined facts form a coherent explanation and whether the competing theory explains them better. Monteen Stover Is Declared Irrelevant Too Quickly Monteen Stover testified that she entered the factory between approximately 12:05 and 12:10 p.m. to collect her pay. She went to Frank’s office and found it empty. This was important because Frank’s early account placed him in the office during that period. The prosecution argued that Stover entered during the interval when Frank had gone into the metal room with Mary. The book later declares Stover’s testimony irrelevant because a streetcar conductor placed Mary’s arrival later than the prosecution claimed. That conclusion is far too absolute. Streetcar testimony involved estimates, routes, stops, and recollections developed months after the event. The defense evidence complicated the prosecution’s timeline, but it did not cause Stover’s observation to vanish. Frank still had to explain why his office was empty during a period when he had said he was there. In his March 1914 jailhouse interview, Frank revisited this problem and suggested that he might have gone to the toilet in the metal room. That statement was significant because the prosecution had placed the murder in or near that area. The book does not give this development the weight it deserves. Lemmie Quinn’s visit is also treated as though it supplied an alibi. It did not account for the entire noon period. A visitor who saw Frank at one point cannot establish his presence during every minute before and after the visit. The proper analysis requires a minute-by-minute reconstruction. The book prefers a broad declaration that the prosecution’s timeline had collapsed. The Medical Disagreement Is Turned into Exoneration Dr. Henry Harris testified about Mary’s facial injuries, the condition of the food in her stomach, and signs of violence in the genital area. Based upon digestion, he estimated that she died approximately thirty to forty-five minutes after eating. Dr. J. W. Hurt disagreed with parts of Harris’s interpretation, particularly concerning genital injury. Defense experts also challenged the digestion estimate. That created a medical dispute. It did not “render the prosecution’s entire timeline invalid,” as the book announces on page 73. Digestion evidence is imprecise. Both sides introduced expert opinion. A disagreement among physicians should be presented as a disagreement, not as the complete destruction of one side’s case. The book also says Harris’s testimony laid the foundation for Dorsey to call Frank a sexual pervert. This phrasing shifts attention away from what Harris testified that he observed and toward an assumed prosecutorial strategy. A reader should be told exactly what each physician found, where they agreed, where they differed, and what limitations applied to their estimates. The book instead converts one defense opinion into an exonerating fact. Jim Conley Is Turned into a Mastermind Whenever the Narrative Requires It No careful reader should deny that Jim Conley lied during the investigation. He gave changing statements and attempted to reduce his own responsibility. The jury knew this. His earlier affidavits, inconsistencies, drinking, criminal history, and admitted falsehoods were examined at length. Luther Rosser cross-examined him for hours. The central question was not whether Conley had ever lied. It was whether the portions of his final account that implicated Frank were corroborated. The book avoids that question by transforming Conley into a highly adaptable criminal genius. He becomes intelligent enough to plan the murder, move the body, invent the notes, manipulate the police, deceive the prosecutor, withstand Rosser’s prolonged cross-examination, and exploit the racial expectations of an all-White jury. At other moments, he is presented as a frightened Black laborer whose statements were gradually constructed by police. These two Conleys are difficult to reconcile. One is the architect of the entire crime and deception. The other is an instrument in the prosecution’s campaign against Frank. The book uses whichever version best removes responsibility from Frank. The fact that police wanted additional statements from Conley does not prove that they supplied the contents. Investigators commonly confront a witness with contradictions and demand a more complete explanation. The important question is whether new details originated with Conley, whether police suggested them, and whether those details matched independently known evidence. The book treats the phrase “we wanted another statement” as nearly conclusive proof of coaching. It is not. The Will Green and William Mincey Stories Are Given More Weight Than They Deserve Page 53 introduces an unnamed carnival worker later identified as Will Green, who supposedly saw Conley attack Mary after a gambling dispute. Investigators could not locate him. He never testified. His identity, reliability, and story were never tested in court. The absence of the witness is then treated as good news for Dorsey, as though the prosecutor benefited from suppressing a dangerous eyewitness. That is speculation. An unlocated person described in a sensational newspaper story is not an eyewitness until he is found, identified, questioned, and tested. William Mincey’s alleged encounter with Conley receives similar treatment. Mincey claimed Conley confessed to killing a girl on the afternoon of April 26. Yet the defense did not call Mincey at trial. That decision is significant. Frank’s lawyers had every reason to present a credible confession by Conley. Their failure to call Mincey suggests that they had concerns about admissibility, credibility, corroboration, or the supposed supporting witnesses. The book admits that the defense never explained the omission, but still presents Mincey’s story as compelling evidence. A sound review would ask why one of Georgia’s most experienced defense teams declined to use a witness who supposedly possessed direct evidence of Conley’s guilt. Recantations and Defense Affidavits Are Treated as Established Truth The chapters concerning Minola McKnight, Dewey Hewell, and other witnesses repeatedly convert disputed later statements into proof that Dorsey manufactured the case. Minola’s treatment by police deserves serious criticism. She was detained and questioned under conditions that would be unacceptable today. Her later repudiation of her affidavit is important. It does not follow that every statement in the affidavit was false or that Dorsey invented its contents. The book uses the same approach with other witnesses. When a witness supported the prosecution in 1913 and later recanted, the recantation is treated as the true account. When the witness later withdrew or contradicted the recantation, the reversal is attributed to threats, pressure, or fear. This again creates a closed system. Statements against Frank are products of coercion. Statements for Frank are products of conscience. A later return to the original account becomes additional evidence of coercion. A reliable history must examine when each statement was made, who was present, what incentives existed, whether the person was under oath, whether cross-examination occurred, and whether independent facts supported the account. The book too often chooses the version favorable to Frank and then explains away the rest. The Racial Interpretation Is Too Simple The book argues that police and prosecutors wanted a White Yankee industrialist rather than a Black laborer because convicting Frank would be a greater achievement. It also argues that an all-White jury believed Conley because racial stereotypes made his lies seem natural and therefore credible. These are possible interpretations. The book presents them as established motives. The racial reality was more complicated. Frank’s defense asked White jurors to reject Black witnesses as liars, criminals, drunkards, and people incapable of reliable reasoning. Conley was attacked through his race as well as through his conduct. Newt Lee was subjected to severe treatment. Minola and Albert McKnight were used by both sides. Black witnesses could be treated as disposable when useful and degraded when inconvenient. Volume 3 of The Secret Relationship Between Blacks and Jews offers a strong counterargument to the conventional pro-Frank treatment of these witnesses. It asks whether modern writers who claim to oppose racism have stripped Black participants of agency by assuming they could only have acted as puppets of White prosecutors. That source is polemical and should not replace the official record. Its strongest point remains valid: a historian should evaluate what Black witnesses said, what they knew, and whether their statements were corroborated. Their testimony should not be accepted or rejected solely through racial theory. The book condemns the racism of 1913 while repeatedly explaining Black testimony as the product of ignorance, manipulation, greed, fear, or criminal cunning. That is not the respectful restoration of Black voices it may appear to be. The Circumcision Theory Is Speculation Presented as Historical Understanding Pages 69 through 71 contain one of the book’s most imaginative claims. Conley testified that Frank had said he was “not built like other men.” The book interprets this as a coded accusation that Frank’s circumcision left him sexually deformed and drove him toward unconventional sexual acts. No witness used the word circumcision. No prosecutor stated that Jewish men were anatomically deformed. No medical evidence was introduced to support such a theory. The book acknowledges that no one stated the claim openly, then proceeds to explain at length what the court supposedly understood. This is not a recovered fact. It is the author’s interpretation of an ambiguous phrase. Conley may have been referring to sexual capacity, physical weakness, reproductive anatomy, or another detail. The phrase may also have been invented. The record does not justify turning it into an unspoken courtroom theory of Jewish genital deformity. The book inserts an antisemitic argument into the trial and then condemns the prosecution for supposedly making it. The Courtroom Crowd Is Described Through an Unverified Slogan On page 61, the book states that people outside the courtroom threatened the jurors with the words, “Hang that Jew, or we’ll hang you!” That exact slogan has become one of the most frequently repeated lines in pro-Frank literature. The book’s source notes do not trace it to a stenographic court record or a clearly identified contemporary witness. They route related claims through Charles and Louise Samuels and Leonard Dinnerstein. There was hostility around the courthouse. There were demonstrations, applause, cheering, and genuine concerns about public order. Those facts should be stated accurately. An emotionally perfect quotation should not be repeated as established fact unless its origin can be identified. The distinction matters because this sentence is used to turn the jury’s decision into the result of a direct death threat. The Georgia Supreme Court reviewed allegations of disorder and the supporting and rebutting affidavits. It did not conclude that the jury had been coerced into conviction. The United States Supreme Court majority later noted that Frank’s claims had been heard repeatedly in the Georgia courts and rejected the federal habeas challenge. Justices Oliver Wendell Holmes Jr. and Charles Evans Hughes dissented and believed the mob-domination allegations deserved further factual examination. Their dissent did not find Frank innocent or identify Mary’s killer. The book presents the contested constitutional argument as though it were the settled history of what happened inside the jury room. The Jury Is Replaced by a Crowd in the Narrative The trial chapters repeatedly contrast defense “facts” with prosecution “emotion.” On page 65, the book says Dorsey understood that a convincing story could not be refuted by facts. On page 73, it says defense testimony invalidated the prosecution’s entire timeline. On page 76, it claims defense witnesses systematically disproved the state’s case. On page 82, it says Arnold and Rosser effectively tore apart Dorsey’s evidence. If all of that were true, the verdict could only be explained by prejudice or fear. That is precisely how the narrative is constructed. The jury disappears as a group of twelve people evaluating weeks of testimony. It becomes an extension of the crowd. The book does not seriously consider that jurors may have believed parts of Conley’s account because they found corroboration. It does not consider that they may have found Frank’s explanations unsatisfactory, Stover credible, the physical evidence meaningful, the murder notes incriminating, or the defense theory incomplete. Instead, it repeatedly tells readers that the jurors were waiting for passion, were unmoved by reason, were impressed by theatrical arguments, and were influenced by mob law. These are conclusions about twelve men’s inner reasoning. The jurors did not leave a collective explanation of their deliberations. The verdict reveals their conclusion, not every thought that led to it. Frank’s Unsworn Statement Is Described Without Its Procedural Advantage Page 80 explains that Frank could not give sworn testimony and undergo ordinary cross-examination under Georgia’s statutory system, but could make an unsworn statement to the jury. He spoke for approximately four hours. The description is technically incomplete because it hides the strategic advantage of the procedure. Frank was permitted to tell his story directly to the jury without taking an oath and without being subjected to the same ordinary cross-examination endured by prosecution witnesses. The book portrays his lengthy discussion of pencil manufacturing and office work as evidence of an analytical personality misunderstood by emotional jurors. Another interpretation is possible. Frank concentrated upon the parts of his account he could control while avoiding hostile questioning about disputed times, his empty office, the metal room, Lee’s schedule, and contradictions in his earlier statements. Choosing the unsworn procedure did not prove guilt. It also did not make his account equivalent to testimony tested by cross-examination. The jury was entitled to consider that difference. Hugh Dorsey Is Psychologized Instead of Answered The book repeatedly explains Dorsey’s actions through personal ambition. It says he needed a major conviction to advance politically. It accuses him of building a story stronger than the facts, coercing witnesses, exploiting sexual rumor, using coded antisemitism, and suppressing evidence favorable to Frank. Some prosecutorial decisions deserve criticism. Dorsey’s methods should be tested against the record. His argument was forceful, emotional, and at times harsh. Yet the book often substitutes an accusation about motive for an answer to the evidence he presented. Dorsey did not ask jurors to believe Conley in isolation. He connected Conley’s account with Frank’s presence, Mary’s pay visit, the office timeline, Stover’s testimony, the notes, the physical evidence, Lee’s schedule, the elevator theory, the basement trail, the medical evidence, and conduct after the discovery. The book rarely reconstructs that combined argument fairly. It describes the prosecution as a web of emotion and prejudice, then congratulates the defense for cutting apart individual strands. A critic cannot disprove a cumulative case by refusing to assemble it. Judge Roan’s Doubt Is Enlarged While His Ruling Is Minimized The book gives great weight to Judge Leonard Roan’s later uncertainty about Frank’s guilt. Those remarks are important and should be included. They should also be placed beside his formal actions. On October 31, 1913, Roan denied Frank’s extensive motion for a new trial. He considered the allegations of courtroom disorder, evidentiary rulings, legal objections, and claims that the verdict was unsupported. He allowed the verdict to stand. The book treats his later discomfort almost as a judicial confession that he had upheld an unjust conviction. It gives much less emphasis to the fact that he had authority to grant a new trial and did not do so. A judge may experience personal doubt while concluding that the legal standard for disturbing a jury verdict has not been met. Doubt is not exoneration. A troubled conscience is not a finding that the defendant was innocent. The Georgia Supreme Court affirmed the conviction. Later state proceedings also failed. The book reduces this history to the suggestion that judges followed technical law rather than common sense. That is rhetoric, not legal analysis. The United States Supreme Court Decision Is Misdated and Misrepresented The timeline says the United States Supreme Court rejected Frank’s appeal on April 9, 1915. Frank v. Mangum , 237 U.S. 309, was decided on April 12, 1915. The majority affirmed the denial of federal habeas corpus relief. The Court stated that Frank had received repeated opportunities to present his claims through Georgia’s judicial system. Holmes and Hughes dissented because they believed the federal court should hear evidence concerning alleged mob domination. The dissent did not retry the murder charge. It did not declare that Conley killed Mary. It did not find Frank factually innocent. The book’s source notes contain an even larger bibliographic error, identifying the case as “237 U.S. 909” and assigning incorrect years in different entries. The correct citation is Frank v. Mangum , 237 U.S. 309 (1915). These are not obscure details. The Supreme Court proceedings are central to the book’s argument that Frank was denied due process. Tom Watson Is Projected Backward into the 1913 Trial Tom Watson later wrote vicious attacks on Frank and used unmistakably antisemitic language. His rhetoric deserves condemnation. The chronology still matters. Watson did not begin publishing about the Frank case until 1914, after the murder, investigation, indictment, trial, verdict, and initial appellate proceedings. His later campaign influenced public opinion surrounding appeals, clemency, commutation, and the aftermath. It cannot be used as direct proof that his rhetoric controlled the jury in August 1913. Pages 99 through 101 place Watson at the center of the “mob spirit” surrounding the trial without maintaining that chronological distinction. The reader is left with the impression that his published campaign helped produce the original conviction. Later hatred cannot simply be projected backward and used to explain an earlier verdict. Governor Slaton Is Presented as the Only Clear-Sighted Authority The treatment of Governor John M. Slaton is openly heroic. The book calls him a man of conscience and says he was the only person in authority willing to ignore emotion and look clearly at the case. Other officials are portrayed as fearful, ambitious, prejudiced, or trapped by legal technicalities. Slaton alone sees the truth. This is hagiography, not balanced history. Slaton conducted a substantial review and issued a detailed commutation statement. His decision deserves careful study. It also deserves context. His law firm had joined with the firm of Luther Rosser, Frank’s lead trial attorney, at the opening of Slaton’s gubernatorial term. That relationship does not prove that the commutation was corrupt. It was politically and ethically significant enough that a balanced account should examine it directly rather than presenting Slaton as a detached outsider. The book also relies upon disputed affidavits, reported confessions, late statements, and material never tested before the trial jury as though Slaton’s consideration transformed them into proven evidence. A commutation is an executive act of mercy or sentence reduction. Slaton changed Frank’s punishment from death to life imprisonment. He did not overturn the conviction, order a new trial, or declare Frank innocent. The timeline dates the commutation to June 20, 1915. Slaton’s formal order was dated June 21, 1915. The Lynching Was Criminal, but It Did Not Prove Innocence Frank’s abduction and lynching on August 17, 1915, were criminal and indefensible. The men who removed him from state custody denied him the protection of law. Georgia failed to protect a prisoner and failed to prosecute his killers. No conclusion about Frank’s guilt can excuse those acts. The book’s account of the lynching is among its strongest sections. It describes the organization of the abductors, the journey to Milledgeville, the removal of Frank, the return to Cobb County, the hanging, and the public reaction. Even here, factual and interpretive problems remain. A photograph on page 120 is captioned as showing that Frank was lynched on the morning of August 16. He was abducted during the night of August 16 and hanged on the morning of August 17. The text also assigns thoughts and meanings to Frank’s last statements. It suggests that his calmness, concern for his wife, and refusal to confess reflected innocence. Those actions may show courage, loyalty, self-control, or innocence. They do not prove which person killed Mary Phagan. A wrongful lynching and a wrongful conviction are separate claims. The first is established. The second remains disputed. The book repeatedly allows the horror of the lynching to flow backward and erase the evidence from the trial. The Anti-Defamation League Claim Is False Pages 124 and 125 state that, after Frank’s lynching, his supporters worked to form the Anti-Defamation League of B’nai B’rith. A caption says the lynching led to the founding of the ADL. The ADL was founded in 1913, two years before Frank’s death. The organization itself has clarified that the Frank case was not the impetus for its founding. Sigmund Livingston had conceived the organization before the case. The trial later reinforced the perceived need for an organization opposing antisemitism, but it did not cause the ADL to be created after the lynching. This is an especially serious error in a book intended to teach history to young readers. The page includes a photograph of a newspaper dated in 1913, which should have alerted the author and editors that the organization existed before August 1915. The Book Oversimplifies the Rebirth of the Ku Klux Klan The same pages state that the Knights of Mary Phagan “reestablished the Ku Klux Klan” and that Frank’s lynching led to the Klan’s reemergence. There was a connection between the Frank controversy and the second Klan. Some men associated with the new order had also been associated with a group described as the Knights of Mary Phagan. Antisemitism arising from the case formed part of the political atmosphere. The book reduces a complicated historical development to a direct act of organizational succession. William Joseph Simmons founded the second Klan in 1915. D. W. Griffith’s The Birth of a Nation , fraternal-order culture, White supremacy, anti-Catholicism, antisemitism, nativism, and the Frank controversy all contributed to the environment. On Thanksgiving night in 1915, Simmons and sixteen other men gathered at Stone Mountain. Several, not necessarily all, had ties to the Knights of Mary Phagan. The book turns influence into sole causation and a disputed organization into the direct founder of a national movement. A young reader will leave with a memorable sentence, but not an accurate understanding of how the second Klan developed. Alonzo Mann Is Called an Eyewitness When He Was a Late Claimant The final chapters depend heavily upon Alonzo Mann’s 1982 affidavit. Mann was eighty-three years old when he claimed that, sixty-nine years earlier, he had entered the factory and seen Conley carrying Mary’s body near the trapdoor. He said Conley threatened him and that his mother ordered him to remain silent. The book calls Mann “the last eyewitness.” He was not an eyewitness to the murder. At most, he claimed to have witnessed Conley carrying the body. That distinction is crucial. Conley had already admitted carrying Mary’s body. Seeing him with the body would contradict parts of his trial account, particularly the location and method of transport. It would not automatically prove that Frank had no role in the killing or cover-up. Mann’s delay also demands serious skepticism. He remained silent during the investigation, coroner’s inquest, trial, motions for a new trial, state appeals, federal proceedings, clemency campaign, Slaton review, and the decades of public controversy that followed. He was never cross-examined about the 1982 account. Investigators could no longer question Conley, Mann’s parents, Frank, the trial lawyers, or most people who had been inside the building. The book says Mann passed two polygraph examinations and treats this as confirmation that he told the truth. Polygraph results are not scientific proof that a historical recollection is accurate. A person may sincerely believe a distorted or reconstructed memory. The book goes further and says Mann’s account could have exonerated Frank and convicted Conley. That conclusion exceeds what the affidavit establishes. Even the 1986 pardon did not adopt Mann’s account as proof of innocence. The 1986 Pardon Is Quoted Correctly but Framed Misleadingly To its credit, the book reproduces the central language of the 1986 pardon. The board expressly stated that it was acting “without attempting to address the question of guilt or innocence.” The pardon recognized Georgia’s failure to protect Frank while he remained in state custody, its failure to preserve his opportunity for continued legal action, and its failure to prosecute his killers. That was a humanitarian pardon. It was not an exoneration. Yet the surrounding chapter places the pardon after Mann’s affidavit, the supposed Conley confession, and other innocence claims. The narrative design encourages readers to treat the pardon as the official conclusion of an innocence campaign. The board deliberately refused to reach that conclusion. The exact language remains controlling. The first pardon application, which more directly implied innocence, was denied on December 22, 1983. The second succeeded because it rested upon the state’s failures surrounding the lynching, not upon a finding that Frank had been wrongly convicted. The A. L. Henson Story Is Untested Hearsay Page 131 says attorney A. L. Henson claimed that Conley confessed to struggling with a girl in the pencil factory and later finding himself in the basement with her dead body. This account appeared decades after the case in Henson’s memoir. Conley was not available for examination. The supposed conversation was not recorded at the time, presented at trial, or tested through cross-examination. The book treats attorney-client privilege as the reason Henson remained silent. That explanation does not transform the story into reliable evidence. It is another example of the book’s unequal standards. A late statement against Conley is accepted as meaningful. Contemporary testimony against Frank is placed under suspicion. Pierre van Paassen’s Legends Dominate the Conclusion Pages 132 and 133 return to van Paassen’s bite-mark story and add further dramatic allegations. The book says he tried to publish proof that Frank’s teeth did not match the wounds. It says someone warned him to abandon the case. It then recounts his claim that a large automobile forced him into the path of a streetcar. These events are presented in smooth narrative prose without independent corroboration. The effect is powerful. The reader imagines hidden forensic evidence, a corrupt prosecutor, threatening messages, and an attempted murder intended to preserve the conspiracy. The proof remains one man’s memoir, published in 1964, concerning events he said occurred in 1922. The book criticizes the 1913 jury for accepting unreliable testimony while using a much lower standard for evidence supporting Frank. The Final Chapters Treat Speculation as Resolution By page 132, the book is no longer asking whether factory witnesses lied. It asks why so many of them lied. That wording assumes the conclusion. It suggests peer pressure, desire for attention, coercion, emotional mass hysteria, and collective delusion. The possibility that some witnesses gave substantially truthful testimony is largely removed. Page 133 asks how a suspect can defend himself when the justice system has been corrupted. Again, corruption is no longer a proposition to be demonstrated. It is the foundation of the question. Page 134 closes with the tenderness of Lucille’s loyalty, the admiration of Frank’s lawyers, and the determination of legal minds to correct injustice. The facing pages then place Mary’s epitaph beside a marker declaring Frank “wrongly accused” and “falsely convicted.” The visual and verbal argument is complete. Mary and Frank are placed together as paired victims, but Frank receives the final declaration of innocence. The book has not proven that declaration. It has arranged the story so that the reader feels it. The Timeline and Reference Material Contain Numerous Errors The timeline and reference sections should have been the easiest parts of the book to verify. They contain a surprising number of mistakes. The book gives May 23, 1913, as the date of Frank’s indictment. The indictment was returned on May 24. It gives April 9, 1915, as the date of the United States Supreme Court decision. The decision was issued on April 12. It says Frank’s execution was rescheduled for June 22, 1916. The correct year was 1915. It places Slaton’s commutation on June 20 rather than June 21. It dates William Creen’s attack to July 17, 1815, an obvious typographical error. It dates the 1986 pardon to March 11, 1985. It identifies Mary in the major-figures section as having been murdered on April 26, 1918. The photograph caption on page 120 dates the lynching to the morning of August 16 rather than August 17. The source notes give an incorrect United States Reports citation for Frank v. Mangum and attach incorrect years to the case. These errors do not all carry equal historical importance. Together, they weaken confidence in a book that asks readers to trust its correction of a complicated legal history. The Photographs Are the Book’s Strongest Feature The book’s greatest value lies in its visual presentation. It contains photographs of Mary Phagan, Leo and Lucille Frank, the National Pencil Company building, lawyers, investigators, jurors, newspapers, the prison farm, the lynching site, and many other people and places connected with the case. The production values are high, and several photographs are reproduced more clearly than in older works. The captions, however, must be checked independently. As the incorrect lynching date demonstrates, a well-reproduced photograph can still carry misleading information. The images make the book worth examining. They do not make the surrounding narrative dependable. Why Mary Phagan-Kean’s Revised Edition Is a Better Starting Point Readers seeking to understand the case should begin with Mary Phagan-Kean’s substantially expanded 2025 edition of The Murder of Little Mary Phagan . Phagan-Kean writes from the Phagan family’s perspective and openly believes that the evidence supports Frank’s conviction. She does not pretend to occupy a position without personal or historical commitments. Her revised work is still a better introduction because it restores the subject that this book gradually displaces: Mary Phagan, the investigation of her murder, the testimony heard at trial, the physical evidence, the appeals, and the difference between conviction, commutation, lynching, pardon, and exoneration. It also requires readers to confront evidence frequently omitted or minimized in pro-Frank accounts. This includes Newt Lee’s changed schedule, the time slip, the murder notes, Monteen Stover’s testimony, Frank’s shifting explanation of the noon period, the second-floor evidence, the basement route, medical testimony, and the extensive appellate record. Phagan-Kean’s conclusions should be tested against the primary sources, just as every other historian’s conclusions should be tested. Her work provides a much fuller foundation from which to begin that comparison. Additional counterpoints include Arthur Burton Rascoe’s The Case of Leo Frank , Francis Xavier Busch’s chapter in Guilty or Not Guilty? , Tom W. Brown’s Notes on the Case of Leo M. Frank and Its Aftermath , and Volume 3 of The Secret Relationship Between Blacks and Jews . Tom Watson’s writings also preserve parts of the contemporary pro-verdict argument, but his antisemitic and inflammatory rhetoric must be separated from any factual or legal claims. His language is not evidence. No secondary book should replace the 1913 Brief of Evidence , the motions and appellate records, the contemporary Atlanta newspapers, the surviving prosecution and defense arguments, and the official pardon decisions. Final Assessment An Unspeakable Crime is not a good book from which to learn the Leo Frank case, it is defense agitprop. It is useful for understanding how the modern pro-Frank narrative is presented to young readers. It shows how Frank can be transformed from a convicted defendant into the central victim of Mary Phagan’s murder story. Its method is consistent. Mary’s biography is handled carelessly. Frank’s biography is enlarged sympathetically. Weak evidence favoring Frank is accepted. Stronger evidence against him is fragmented or omitted. Dorsey’s motives are attacked. The jurors’ thoughts are invented. Late recantations are elevated, but no mention of how they were induced is mentioned. Contemporary testimony is distrusted. Executive commutation is treated as moral vindication. A humanitarian pardon is positioned near exoneration. The criminal injustice of the lynching is allowed to erase the unresolved question of factual guilt. The book’s author plainly researched the case and visited important archives. The problem was not an absence of effort. It was the direction of that effort. She entered the research already convinced that Frank had suffered a travesty of justice, then organized the surviving record around that conviction. Its strongly partisan pro-Frank perspective leads it to emphasize information that supports its conclusion while giving insufficient attention to evidence that complicates or challenges that interpretation. The book belongs beside Leonard Dinnerstein, Harry Golden, and Charles and Louise Samuels as part of an established tradition of extreme pro-Frank advocacy. It does not introduce readers to the full controversy. It initiates them into one side of it. Its clear prose, striking photographs, and attractive design may give the impression of authority, but the numerous factual mistakes, unsupported legends, selective source use, imagined motives, chronological errors, and missing prosecution evidence tell a different story. The photographs introduce the faces. The narrative has already assigned the halos and horns. The essential rule for studying the case should be simple: establish the facts first, then form the interpretation. An Unspeakable Crime too often reverses that order, selecting the information that best supports its argument while giving insufficient scrutiny to claims that are disputed, weakly sourced, or unsupported by the surviving record. Souvanna is not at all sanguine that an early settle- ment among the three princes can be arranged. He suspects that Phoumi will attempt to stall on a conference site and on conditions. Phoumi has already indicated that before any meeting he would require "firm assurances" that, in a coalition government, all im- portant decisions of the interior and defense ministries would the USSR will be forced to answer in kind with tests of "new types" of its nuclear weapons. In a speech last December Khrushchev claimed that the USSR, as a result of its tests in the fall, "obtained a mighty new weapon"--thermonuclear bombs with a power of 50 to 100 mega- tons and more. This statement follows a pattern the Chinese have used before in hopes that raising the specter of Chinese intervention would forestall further US military moves in the area. Throughout the Laotian crisis, Peiping had repeatedly intimated that Chinese Nation- alist irregulars could provide a pretext for Chinese Communist military intervention. On 2 April 1961, Foreign Minister Chen Yi stated that if SEATO forces moved into Laos, the Chinese Communists would respond by sending in their own forces. In connection with this state- ment, Chen also cited the threat Nationalist irregulars allegedly posed for China's security. In the 16 May commentary, People's Daily threatened no action more specific than height- ened vigilance and made no reference to threats to the security of China. Government forces--driven from Nam Tha on 6 May--withdrew across northwest Laos to the town of Ban Houei Sai on the Mekong River. The move from Nam Tha--characterized by poor leadership and a total organi- zational breakdown--once more provided firm evidence of the impotence of government forces when confronted by well-led and well-disciplined troops. The Pathet Lao - North Vietnamese forces apparently declined to exploit their military advantage at Ban Houei Sai; a recent ground reconnaissance to a distance of 15 miles east of the town did not reveal the presence of enemy troops. General Phoumi, apparently discouraged regarding the chances of recovering northern Laos, has indicated that his main defense effort will be centered south of the Nam Ca Dinh River in central Laos. In northern Laos, such bases as Luang Prabang, Vientiane, and Sayaboury would be retained 25X1 as centers from which extensive guerrilla warfare operations would be conducted. CHINESE REFUGEE PROBLEM AT HONG KONG The number of refugees from South China to Hong Kong sharply increased during the past week, and Peiping is making no effort to stem the flow. In the past the Hong Kong police ordinarily arrested one or two hundred il- legal border crossers a month. In the month of April the figure jumped to 1,500, and in the first two weeks of May, over 17,000 were apprehended--4,543 on 14 May alone. These figures in- clude only those attempting to cross the 15-mile land frontier between China's Kwangtung Prov- ince and the British colony; large numbers are also attempt- ing to come in by sea. The Hong Kong authorities are sending back most of the boarder crossers they apprehend, and as of 15 May the Chinese Communists were still accepting them. Many of the refugees, however, are remaining in the border area to try again. The size of the groups making the crossing is growing; the border guards had to use force to bring into custody a rowdy band of 2,500 refugees on 13 May. As thousands gather in the vicinity of the border the British authorities have be- come increasingly concerned over the possibility of an ugly incident. It is as yet difficult to determine just why the bans on emigration have been lifted. Previously it had been hard to obtain exit permits from SECRET 18 May 62 WEEKLY REVIEW Page 4 of 18 Approved For Release 2008/05/16: CIA-RDP79-00927AO03600070001-7 Approved For Release 2008/05/16: CIA-RDP79-00927AO03600070001-7 X11/ JliVitLJ- ~~I Communist China, but in April public security officials in Canton, Kwangtung's capital, were told to process as many permits as possible for persons wanting to emigrate to Hong Kong or nearby Portuguese Macao. They were told that the reason for the change in policy was the necessity of further reducing urban population and the un- desirability of sending any more city residents to the countryside. Most of the refugees are young adults from farming dis- tricts near Hong Kong. Inter- rogation of the refugees has disclosed that local Communist officials asked the refugees to remain in China but did not prevent their leaving. Observa- tions at the border show that in many cases border guards actually helped the refugees to cross. The about-face in Communist policy may stem from the real- ization that, in Kwangtung at least, there are too many mouths to feed and it is better to allow surplus population to be siphoned off, at least from those areas where Hong Kong presents a ready alternative. In addition, the officials may be chary of taxing their public security control apparatus by trying to stanch the flow, pre- ferring to let the Hong Kong authorities bear the onus for this. The refugees themselves give hunger as their reason for leaving; however, the British report that the majority appear in good health, although lean. This is the time of the year when food stocks throughout China are at their tightest; rations have reportedly been cut recently in some areas just to the east of Hong Kong which were particularly hard hit by weather last year. The harvest of early rice in Kwangtung is four to six weeks off, although some early vegetables are prob- ably ripening now. The responses of the ref- ugees correspond with the answers given in a recent poll of Chi- nese students by the Hong Kong Government. Out of some 3,600 such students who were allowed by the Communists to visit rel- atives in Hong Kong during the Chinese New Year's vacation last February, about 3,100 have refused to return in the main- land. The principal reason given was hard living condi- tions in China. In the opinion of the US Consulate General in Hong Kong, the decision of such large numbers to abandon their mainland education represents a vote of no confidence by the students in the future prospects of the Peiping regime. Under present circumstances, Hong Kong officials believe that they have no alternative but to return as many refugees as possi- ble. Despite a prosperous economy, the colony is hard pressed to provide work for a growing labor force. Opportunities for resettlement of Chinese abroad are severely restricted. The government is spending 33 percent of its budget for so- cial services. Out of a burgeon- ing population of over 3,000,000, an estimated 1,000,000 are ref- ugees in need of some assistance. A high government official has said the border situation is still under control, but the flow cannot be reduced to manageable proportions without help from the Communist author- ities. He despaired of trying to build bigger and better fences to hold back the refugees unless such barriers are backed up by "the kind of force the Hong Kong government strongly desires not to use." ag,anda . The British oppose any ac- tion that would irritate the Chi- nese Communists. They believe Chinese Nationalist efforts to expand the role of the UN High Commissioner for Refugees in Hong Kong are likely to aggravate the situation. They have stepped up efforts to disrupt rail and road communica- tions and demonstrated increased willingness to engage regular South Vietnamese units. Civil Guard and Self-Defense Corps posts, however, continue to be prime targets, and there have been several attacks recently against the government's land- development centers and construc- tion projects, which are fre- quently defended by such forces. Government troops continue to report heavy Viet Cong casual- ties and the destruction of Viet Cong installations as the result of airstrikes and operations by airborne troops. The Viet Cong are showing increased effective- ness with small arms fire against helicopters while they are land- ing or taking off in guerrilla- infested areas. Curtailment of rail traffic and the danger of road ambush are leading to fur- ther government reliance on air communications. During the past wo weeks, one province in the Second Corps area was the scene of repeated bridge sabotage and a direct attack on a repair train; two train derailments in the First Corps zone resulted in one case in heavy casualties in a Civil Guard contingent which was being moved south. There is little firm infor- mation on the extent of infil- tration from North Vietnam. Both sides agree on going ahead with the referendum scheduled for 1 July. The PAG fears, however, that the French re- luctance to force a showdown with the OAS means that sup- pressing the organization will be left to the Algerian Na- tional Army (ALN)--thereby enhancing that element's po- litical role after the referen- dum. Both French and PAG au- thorities recognize that the terrorism will probably not be stopped by 1 July. About 300, or 70 percent, of the "professional" OAS terrorists in the Algiers region have been arrested, ou-c terrorism continues-to increase. The "professionals" have been replaced by youths who have been encouraged in disrespect for law by their environment in recent years. They have no police records, however, and their age limits police efforts to cope with them as a group. Efforts are under way to handle this prob- lem by having the government draft all males between 18 and 25 years old in Algiers and Oran. High Commissioner Fouchet is reportedly resigned to con- tinued opposition to the Evian accords from the European population in Algeria. The government's determination to proceed with the referendum is nevertheless evident in reports that the small staff under Minister for Algerian Affairs Joxe is concentrating on the mechanics of setting it up. Increasingly tough meas- ures to curb terrorism are being implemented, but short of an all-out military sub- jection of Algiers and Oran, which responsible authorities are loath to push, voting may not be possible in those cities. Joxe and President Fares of the Provisional Executive agree that a massive pro-independence vote will be forthcoming from the rest of Algeria. At the same time, the left wing of international Communism, led by Peiping, had begun to challenge the USSR. Khrushchev had to move gradually lest his dealings with Tito give sub- stance to Chinese charges of Soviet "revisionism." Khru- shchev probably calculated that there was no longer much possibility of reconciling his differences with the left wing SECRET 18 May 62 Approved For Release 2008/05/16: CIA-RDP79-00927A003600070001-7 )f 9 Approved For Release 2008/05/16: CIA-RDP79-00927AO03600070001-7 CURRENT INTELLIGENCE WEEKLY SUMMARY and, therefore, was not con- cerned that his improved rela- tions with Tito would make such a reconciliation more remote. for Yugoslavia's growing industry, enhance the importance of Yugo- slavia's voice in international affairs, and proselytize his own brand of Communism. When Yugoslavia refused to submit to Moscow's discipline in 1958, the bloc ceased grant- ing the Yugoslav state preferred treatment. In May of that year, all bloc developmental loans were canceled, and the Yugo- slavs were no longer invited to meetings of the bloc's international economic organiza- tion (CEMA), in which Belgrade had observer status. Neverthe- less, normal state functions were maintained, trade continued, and cultural, scientific, and trade union delegations moved back and forth, if with decreased regularity. Communist China and Al- bania, however, found common ground in a violent anti-Yugo- slav policy. As a result, respective diplomatic missions were eventually left in the hands of charges, and Yugoslavia's trade with these countries dwindled to virtually nothing. Yugoslav-Albanian relations be- came particularly tense by late 1960, with border incidents and publicized spy trials. Tito, in an effort to prevent this situation from leading again to Yugoslavia's complete political and economic isolation from the bloc, argued that ideological differences should not harm interstate relations. Belgrade's half- hearted efforts to build up relations with the West had proven only partially satis- factory. In 1959, Yugoslavia refused to provide information on intended use of US military equipment under negotiation,, and US military aid to Yugo- slavia was terminated at Bel- grade's request. Tito's primary effort was devoted to developing his ties with the nonaligned states, whose number was rapidly in- creasing. He hoped that by again identifying with these states, he could secure markets In late 1958 Tito under- took his first of several visits to numerous uncommitted states. He succeeded in assuming a position of leadership in this group, as illustrated by the convocation in Belgrade of a conference of heads of state from the nonaligned countries in September 1961. In this position, the Yugoslavs view themselves as competitors of both the East and West and do not hesitate to criticize either. By the time of the UN session in September 1960--when Tito and Khrushchev met for the first time since 1957--Khru- shchev had apparently decided that improved relations with Tito could be turned to Soviet ad- vantage. Tito had, despite his differences with Moscow, continued to agree with Soviet foreign policies on almost all issues not directly affecting Yugoslav national interests or those of another nonaligned state. In addition, Belgrade had by this time made abundantly clear its violent opposition to the policies of the Chinese Communists, who were challenging the USSR for influence in Asia, Africa, and Latin America. Khrushchev's decision paid off in September 1961, when at the Belgrade conference Tito defended the Soviet resumption of nuclear testing and Khrushchev's aggressive German policy. The marked similarities in Yugoslav and Soviet foreign policies result in part from a common Marxist orientation. Belgrade views "socialism" as the wave of the future and capitalism as a dying anachronism; therefore, bloc policies toward the West are by definition "pro- gressive." At the same time, there is an area of common national interest: as a result of its World War II experience, Belgrade believes that peace in Europe and its own security are served by a weak, divided Germany. SuT 18 May 62 SPECIAL ARTICLES Page 2 of 9 Approved For Release 2008/05/16: CIA-RDP79-00927AO03600070001-7 Approved For Release 2008/05/16: CIA-RDP79-00927AO03600070001-7 SECRET CURRENT INTELLIGENCE WEEKLY SUMMARY Finally, Yugoslavia's pursuit of favor with the nonaligned states leads it to assume violent anti-Western, "anticolonial" positions. Yugoslavia's state relations with Moscow's European satellites have not improved apace. While East European leaders on appro- priate occasions call for im- proved state relations, and dele- gations are more frequently ex- changed, no important develop- ments have resulted and friction- al incidents still take place. Belgrade lodged a "most severe" protest with the East Germans in mid-March for forcibly re- moving from trains Yugoslav officials who were returning from the Leipzig Fair. This situation apparently reflects the individual bias of the satel- lite leaders and also suggests a lack of Soviet directives or- dering them to improve their relations with Yugoslavia. Economic Relations Performance under long-term trade agreements signed in 1961 has not matched expectations. The Yugoslav-Soviet pact scheduled a 100-percent increase by 1965, but total trade with the bloc, after rising somewhat in 1960, fell back in 1961 to around 1959 levels. Trade with indi- vidual bloc countries was so uneven, moreover, that substan- tial surpluses of trade were registered with the USSR and Poland, while equally substantial deficits occurred with Hungary, Czechoslovakia, and East Germany. Belgrade has claimed that the recent purchases of Soviet military equipment were a straight commercial deal to utilize its trade credit with the USSR. Belgrade has charged that the bloc refuses to sell Yugo- slav importers the high-quality commodities they want. The bulk of the blame, however, probably lies with Yugoslavia, which is economically oriented toward the West. Yugoslav im- porters and exporters prefer dealing with the West, and im- plementation of a trade liberal- ization program early last year gave them greater flexibility to buy and sell where they wished. Belgrade will have to re-establish more direct con- trols over the national economy if trade with the bloc is to be substantially increased. Party Relations International Communism, for all practical purposes, broke off party relations with the Yugoslavs when all bloc ambassadors but Poland's who were attending the Yugoslav party's seventh congress in April 1958 walked out on the proceedings. There are no in- dications that these relations will be resumed soon. Since the Soviet party's 22nd congress last October, such a ranking bloc figure as Czech party First Secretary Novotny stated also that as long as the Yugo- sla,vs "adhere to their revision- ist theses, there can be no normalization of relations along party lines"--words subsequently echoed by Bulgaria's Zhivkov. A Soviet official in late March claimed in a public lecture to a Soviet audience that Bel- grade had requested a restitu- tion of party ties but had been rebuffed. The sole violator of the international movement's ban on party relations with Yugoslavia is the Italian Communist party, whose leader, Palmiro Togliatti, is a noted proponent of polycentrism. In the past six months, the Italians have sent at least two party dele- gations to Yugoslavia, at least one of which discussed ideolog- ical questions. Ideology Underlying Belgrade's ideological differences with the bloc is Yugoslavia's re- fusal to subordinate its na- tional interests to those of the Soviet Union and recognize the USSR as the supreme inter- preter of Marxism-Leninism. Moreover, as specific ideolog- ical points are disputed they become a source of conflict in themselves. The critical exchanges with Moscow accompanying the SECRET 18 May 62 SPEC:TAT.
